cells.tense: You are here, keeping something small alive and marking it with other people.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing that grew this week and tell two people about it, out loud.
cells.core:
This is what you do best. Something is growing under your hands, and instead of rushing it toward the finish you stay next to it and let it be small for as long as it needs. That patience is not softness. It is the whole reason things take root around you.

And then you mark it. Something goes well and you gather the people who were in it and say so. Joy like that doesn't stay where it's made — it moves through the room and comes back bigger. You keep that going, and the effort stays quiet. Nothing about it feels forced. What holds it steady is that when you celebrate, you mean it, and it gathers the people who were already inside the thing.
cells.sheetLine: You tend the small thing, then mark it with the people in it.
cells.verb: Raising joy together and letting it spread
cells.place: Beside what is still small and not finished

cells.tense: You are already at the moment after it works, bracing for a future that has not been written yet.
cells.ask: Let one thing stay unfinished this week and tell no one how it will turn out.
cells.core:
Right now you are pushing what is growing toward a moment that hasn't arrived. The celebration is already being planned in your head — who will be there, how good it will be — before the thing has had time to become itself. You are feeding it the ending instead of the day.

That push has a cost. Things that grow on their own schedule get pulled off it, and the joy gets made into a verdict on whether you were right to force it. Let the harvest keep its own clock. You'll be standing in it when it's ready, and the people you gather will be celebrating the thing that grew rather than a version that hasn't happened.
cells.sheetLine: You're celebrating the harvest before you've grown it.
cells.verb: Raising joy together and letting it spread
cells.place: Beside what is still small and not finished

cells.tense: You are still standing where something was marked and did not go well, and you have stopped raising anything to be marked.
cells.ask: Name one small thing going well out loud to someone — not a big one, one that feels almost too small to count.
cells.core:
You know how to celebrate — it has not gone anywhere. What has changed is the raising: things that should mark themselves pass quietly, and you call it not making a fuss. The crowd around you stays just outside the door.

But what is growing in your care still needs the mark. It needs someone to say this happened and it was good. The room doesn't have to be full. It has to exist. Start by saying one small thing out loud, badly if that's what it takes. The joy may have been there the whole time; the door out where anyone could hear it is the part that is closed.
cells.sheetLine: The celebrations stopped. It was never that there was nothing to mark.
cells.verb: Raising joy together and letting it spread

cells.tense: You are already pulling people into shared joy, and talking about it as if it were happening around you.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person, 'I made this good moment.' Use your own name.
cells.core:
Look at what happens around you when something goes well. People come together around it, and it gets bigger because they do. You call that the mood, the timing, the group — anything but yours. But the thing that makes a moment shared is the choice to share it. The invitation, the announcement, the steady hand on the thing that was still growing. That's you.

The work has been running the whole time. Your name just hasn't been on it. When you gather those thoughts into one place and finally say what you did, the recognition doesn't swell your head. It settles you, and the next celebration stands on something truer. The door is already open. Step through it as the one holding it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already gathering people into joy. You call it the moment, not your doing.
cells.verb: Raising joy together and letting it spread

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has ever been mocked or punished for joy — the Too Little cell must not add a before, a who, or a how long ago. A reader could reasonably reply that they do celebrate, just selectively, and that raising small things feels like a start rather than an emptiness. The asks survive a wrong read because they only add something small, and nothing in them depends on that read. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is 'the sorting that picks what's worth marking' — it sounds like a built method; the cell now marks something plain and small instead.
